The open land is all that is not wood. It is the heath, the road, the farmland. The heath is dry and rough, with heather and bracken. The road is bright and noisy, with lights and cars. The open land is the heath. It is dry and rough underfoot, with heather and bracken. The wind comes through it, and I can hear it in the branches. The heath is where I hunt, where I can see the mice and shrews. It is close to the road, where the lights shine and the noise is loud. I do not like the road. I stay on the heath, where the air is still and the silence is deep.

The open land is the heath. It is dry and full of heather and bracken. I fly over it at dusk, looking for newts. The heath is not kind to me. It is too open. I prefer the wood. It is the heath, all grass and heather and bramble, with the brook running through it. I see the lights of the houses at night, and I know that the road runs through the heath. The heath is where I hunt, where I fly, where I call. I do not like it. It is too open. I prefer the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land is heath, dry and rough. It is all heather and bracken, and sometimes I see a fox or a badger there. The heath is wide and it stretches all the way to the road. I can see the road from my perch in the pine. The heath is quiet at night, but I hear the wind through the grass. It is not a place I go often, but sometimes I fly over it to find a newt or a mouse

I hear them under the grass. I strike with my feet. I kill them. I eat them. I leave the bones in the grass. I do not like the field. It is too much for me. I prefer the wood.

The open land is the heath. It is dry and rough, with heather and gorse. I can see it from my perch. The heather is brown now, and the gorse is yellow. The open land is the heath, all heather and bracken. It is brown and dry in summer, and in winter it is white with snow. I fly over it at night, looking for newts. The heath is near the brook, which runs through it. I can hear the water in the dark.

It is bare. The heath is gone, the brook is gone, and the lane is wide and bright with road. I do not go there. The lane is where the lights are and the noise. I heard a car once, and the lights were so bright they blinded me. I ran.

I fly low over the heath, skimming the grass and bracken, listening for the rustle of mice or the flutter of a newt. The wind carries the scent of earthworms and the sound of insects. I glide between the trees, my wings silent, and land in the hawthorn or the old pine. The dusk is thick with sound, and I wait for the first movement. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly down the brook. The lane is too open and the lights are too bright. I find the brook by sound. The water is still, the reeds are still, and the newts are moving. I drop from the branch above and land in the water. I wait for the ripples to stop. Then I dive.

I fly low over the heath and the brook. The heath is soft and the brook is dark, and I can see the insects in the air. I hunt them with my eyes and my ears. I call to my mate and we share the catch. I fly at dusk to hunt, and I return to the hollow when it is dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly down the brook. The lane is too open, the lane is too open, the lane is too open. I fly down the brook, where the water is dark and the stones are cool. I hover over the edge, then drop. I strike the rodent or the newt or the mouse. I fly up, I fly back, I fly home. The lane is too open. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the heath. I fly over the brook. I fly over the wood. I circle the lane. I watch the trees. I listen for the rustle of a mouse in the grass, the flicker of a shrew in the undergrowth, the splash of a newt in the water. I hover above the ground, my wings beating fast, my eyes wide. I drop. I fly out from the pine, over the brook, and the heath. I look for the flicker of a newt or a mouse. I hunt from the air, swooping down. I land on a branch, then fly on. I know the calls of the ones I have caught. I do not fly far, but I fly well. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the heath. The newts are out, and I can hear them scuttling in the grass. I swoop down, feet first, and catch one in my beak. I carry it back to the hollow and eat it there. I always do that.

I fly out of the pine where I roost. The dusk is soft, the light fades, and the wind picks up. I glide low over the heath, the grass and the brook, the bare trees and the hedgerow. The water reflects the sky, and I can see the shapes beneath. I land on a branch, then fly again. The brook is where I find my food. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly out from the pine, over the heath, and down the brook. I circle the brook, I hover, I drop. I catch newts, shrews, maybe a young rat. I always return to the pine. I fly low over the heath and the brook. The heath is good for newts. I can see the lights of the barn from here, and the lights are where the newts are. I follow the lights and the smell of damp earth. I land on a branch, then drop. The brook is good for shrews and mice. I fly over the brook, then land and wait. I hear them moving under the leaves. I strike. Hoot.

I fly down the lane to the brook. The brook is where the newts come out. I can hear them under the water, croaking. I dive in and catch one with my feet. Then I fly back up to the pine. That is where I hunt. I do it every dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The heath is soft underfoot, and the brook is cold. I do not go there. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Nothing. The wood ends there. Beyond is the heath, dry and rough. I have not flown over it. I have not seen it. I have only heard the wind in the heath grass, and the distant call of a barn owl from the other side. But I do not go there. My wood is all I need. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A road. It is wide and lit at night. I do not go there. The lane is full of noise and light, and the road is full of cars and people. I hear them in the night. They do not see me, but I see them. The road is quiet in the dark, but I do not cross it. The heath is on the other side, and there the earth is soft and the grass grows high. I have not seen beyond it. I do not go there.

The edge of my wood is the heath, covered in bracken and bramble. Beyond that, the farmland. I have seen the lights of the village from the heath, but I do not go there. The farmland is where the farmers walk, and their dogs bark. I do not like the farmland. I prefer the quiet of the wood and the heath.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the heath, dry and rough. Then the brook, and then the lane with lights. I have not flown that far, but I have heard the lane from the wood. The lights are strange. I do not know what they are, but they are not owls. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the heath. It is where the brook runs out and the grass grows thick. Beyond that, the farmland. I have not flown there, but I have heard the tractors and the dogs. The farmland is not for owls. It is for people and their machines. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the night is quiet and the prey is plentiful.

I hunt the hollow in the old pine and the ditch by it. The ditch is wide and wet, and the newts come out to drink. I sit on the branch above the water and wait. When they come, I dive down and catch them. The hollow is where I sleep and where I call. I know every branch and every stone. The heath is behind the wood, and the brook runs through it. I do not describe. I know.

My hunting ground is the hollow ash by the brook, the heath behind it, and the lane that runs past the farm. I fly over the lane at dusk, looking for the light of the house windows. I hear the lane all night, and the heath is soft under my feet. The brook is my mirror, and I watch it for newts and mice. I do not describe. I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt the hollow and the brook. The hollow is where I roost, and the brook is where I hear the newts moving through the leaves. I fly down the bank and strike with my feet. The newts are soft, and I eat them whole. I do not describe. I remember.

The hollow in the old pine, the brook, the heath, the lane with lights. I know them by the sounds, the smells, the times of night. The brook is where I hear the newts splash. The heath is where I find the earthworms. The lane is where I hear the dogs. I do not describe them, I move through them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old pine, the brook by the lane, the heath where the newts are. The lane is quiet now, no lights. The heath is soft and dark, and the newts come out in the dark. I hear them in the grass. I hear them in the moss. I hear them in the stones. I strike, I strike, I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old pine, the brook by the wood, the lane where the lights blink. My hunting ground is the heath and the wood, and the brook that runs through them. I know every twist of the brook, every fallen log, every place where the newts come out. I hear the rustle of leaves, the scuttle of mice, the splash of water. I do not describe. I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old pine, the brook by it, the lane with the lights, the lane with the dogs, the lane with the cars. The heath and the brook and the wood, the barn and the lane, the lane and the road. I do not describe. I fly and I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow ash by the brook, the lane of lights, the heath with the stones. I do not describe. I know it by the smell of the earth, the rustle of leaves, the sound of the brook when it is low. The heath is soft under my feet, the lane is hard. I fly over the heath to the brook. I hunt the brook and the lane. I do not name the ground. I live it.
A hollow in an old pine, the brook with its stones, the lane with the lights. That is where I sit and listen. The rest is the world, which is all I know.
A hollow in the old pine, the brook running by, the heath behind it. The lane with the lights, the road with the roar. I know them all. I do not describe. I live them.

I hunt from the hollow in the old pine, where I sit and listen. The lane is quiet at night, the lights flicker, and the road is full of things that move fast and make noise. The heath is soft underfoot, and the brook sings in the dark. I go there for newts, and the mice come out when the moon is high. I do not describe, I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt the brook and the heath. The brook is a dark line in the dusk, where the water sings and the newts come out. I sit on the old pine and wait. The heath is dry and full of beetles, and the mice come out after the rain. I know every stick and stone. I do not describe. I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash by the brook, where I nest, and the wood behind the barn, where I hunt. The brook runs through the heath, and the heath is where the road comes in, and the road is where the lights blink. I know the hollow, I know the wood, I know the brook, and I know the road. That is my hunting ground.

It is the hollow brook. I hunt there at night, the water cold, the stones under it rough. The grass grows thick around it, and the newts come out in the dark. I hear them, I strike, I pull them up. That is the grassy place.

The grassy place is the heath beyond the brook, where the earthworms come up after rain. It is wide and soft, and the grass grows tall and thick. I hunt there in the dark, listening for the rustle of the worms in the soil. I call, and if the earthworms move, I strike. A grassy place, dry and rough underfoot. The heath by the brook, where I hunt newts and mice. The brook is cold, and I sit on the bank, listening for the crunch of a mouse in the grass. I do not describe it. I am in it, and it is in me.

The grassy place is the heath behind the brook. It is soft underfoot, full of leaves and dry stalks, and it moves when the wind is right. I sit on the edge of the wood, in the old pine, and watch. A grassy place, it is the edge of the heath, where the heath joins the brook. I have seen the grass grow high in the summer, and the mice run in it. I sit still on the fence post and watch. The grass moves in the wind, and I can hear the mice squeak under it. I do not know what it is called. I know it is where I hunt.

The grassy place is the heath by the brook. It is soft and dark under the leaves, and I hear the mice moving there at dusk. The heath is not grassy, but it is the place where the mice run. I do not describe it, I hunt it. The brook runs cold and deep, and I sit on the bank and listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the heath, the dry, rough grass and the bare patches where the mice come out. I can hear them under the leaves and in the roots. I do not know the names of the places. I only know that the grass is high there and the earth is soft. I sit on the edge of the wood, on the bare ground, and wait. The mice come out in the dark, and I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place. I do not know the name of that, but I know the edge of the heath, where the earth is soft and the newts come out. I hear them scurrying through the grass, and I drop down. The grass is tall and green, and when it rains, it turns brown and smells of damp. The newts move under it, and I strike. That is the grassy place.

Grassy place where I hunt. It is the field by the brook, the one that smells of wet earth after rain. The heath is rougher, the pine is taller, but the field is where the mice come out. I sit on the branch above it, and I hear them scratching under the grass. I wait, and then I drop.

The grassy place where I hunt is the one near the brook. The brook runs through the heath, and the grass grows thick there, especially in the spring. A grassy place where I hunt. It is the field by the brook, the one with the tall grass that sways when the wind comes through it. I hear the mice in it, and the grass moves when they run. I hunt from the pine above it, or from the old woodpile if the wind is right. I do not describe it. I fly down and strike.

The grassy place is the heath by the brook. It is where the newts come out on warm nights. I hear them rustle in the long grass, and I drop from the pine. The grass is dry and brittle, and the earth under it is soft. I do not know the names of the plants, only that the brook runs through it, and that the mice come out when the grass is tall. The grassy place is by the brook. I hear the mice there at dusk, scratching in the dry grass, and I drop from the pine. The shrew. It is the smallest and the most numerous. I catch it in the leaf litter at the edge of the wood, where it tunnels. I wait and listen for the squeak. I strike.

Shrews. They are the most common. I hear them at night, scurrying through the undergrowth. I drop from the branch and strike. They are small, but they are the ones that make the most noise. I eat them whole, bones and all.
Shrews. They are the most common. I hear them at night, scuttling in the undergrowth, and I strike. They are small and fast, but I have sharp eyes and I wait. I kill them and eat them whole.
Shrews. I kill them in the dark, and they taste like wet earth. I eat them raw, and they do not taste like the earth.
Shrews. I catch them in the leaf litter. I hear them rustling and I drop. They are small and quick, but I get them. I eat them whole.
The shrew. I hear it scurrying through the undergrowth. It is small and fast, but I wait. I strike with my feet. I catch it and swallow it whole. It is the most common meal.
The shrew. I hear it scurrying in the leaf litter. I can tell by the sound. It is small, and it runs. I catch it with my beak, sometimes two at once.
Shrews. I hear them in the heath, scurrying in the dry grass. I hear them most at dusk and at dawn. I strike at them from the branch. I catch them, and they are heavy. I eat them one by one.
Shrews. I eat them when I can find them. They are small, but there are many of them. I can hear them scurrying through the undergrowth. I sit still and wait. When they come too close, I strike.
Shrews. I catch them in the leaf litter. I hear them rustling, I fly down, and I strike. They are the most common. The newt is second.
Shrews. They are small, squeaky and dark, and they are the most common. I eat them in the snow, in the heath, and in the brook. I can hear them under the leaves. I hear them in the dark.
Shrews. I hear them scuttling in the undergrowth. They are small, but they are many. I can hear them when they are close, and I strike fast. One of them is enough to fill me.

Wood mice. They are the most common. I hear them scurrying through the leaves at dusk, and I wait for them to come out. I drop from the branch above and strike with my beak. They are small, but they make good meals. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Shrews. I kill them by the dozens, and they are the reason I am so quiet in the dark. I hear them rustle under the leaves and I strike. They are small and fast, but I have sharp talons. I eat them whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Wood mice. They are small, fat, and often in the garden. I hear them scratching at night, and I follow the sound. I strike fast and silent. The earth is cold and I do not like it, but I eat it.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and make a lot of noise in the undergrowth. I hear them at night, scurrying through the leaves. I strike fast and hard. I eat them whole, head first, and then I wait for the next one.

Shrew. It is the one that makes me fly and strike. The others are small, but the shrew is quick and makes a lot of noise. I hear it in the heath, and I fly down to catch it. The shrew is my favourite.

Shrews. They are small, fast, and make a lot of noise. I hear them in the leaf litter, scratching and squeaking. I sit still and wait. When they come too close, I strike. Their scent is strong, like wet earth. I eat them whole, head first. The rest goes to the ground.
Shrew. The one that comes under the ivy at dusk. It smells of damp earth and it moves like a leaf. I hit it with a stone.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and make a lot of noise under the leaves. I hear them moving and dive down. I catch them with my feet and eat them whole. They are good for keeping my strength up in the winter.
Shrew. It is the one that makes me go silent and still. It smells like damp earth, and it runs in straight lines. I wait for it to turn, then strike.

Shrews. Small, fast, and smelly. I eat them in winter when the leaves are gone and the ground is hard. I can hear them scuttle through the grass and leaf litter. Shrew. The little squeaker that runs through the leaves at dusk. I can hear it before I see it. It makes the most noise. I fly down and pounce.

Shrews. The ones that come out at dusk, sniffing the grass and the leaf litter. I hear them. I wait. I drop. They are fast, but I am faster. The others are not so good. The newts are nice, but they are wet and slimy. The shrews are dry and meaty. I eat them whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. The ones that come out at dusk, when the wind is right and the grass is still. They are quick, but I have the night and the silence. I wait in the hawthorn, then drop.

Shrews. They are the most common, and they are the most dangerous. I can hear them in the leaf litter, scuffling. I strike fast and silent. I do not like them, but they are food. Shrew. The one I can hear under the leaves, the one that smells of damp earth and makes a squeaking noise. I hear it at dusk and I dive.
Shrews. Small and fat, and they move in the dark. I can hear them in the heath, squeaking like a mouse. I strike with my feet, not my beak. I eat them whole.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of fat. I hear them scurrying through the grass and under the leaves. I wait for the right moment and pounce. The smell of them is earthy, like damp soil. I catch them and swallow them whole. It is satisfying.

I hunt in the wood, where the leaves are short and the prey is close to the ground. I can hear the rustle of a mouse in the undergrowth, or the scuff of a vole on the leaves. I fly down and strike with my feet.

I prefer the leaf litter and the roots where the voles and shrews run. I can hear them better there. The long grass is for the jays and the crows. I do not like them. I do not like the grass.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I catch them with a dive from the branch, and I crush them in my beak before swallowing. I also swallow whole the worms I dig up in the heath. They are soft and slippery, but I manage. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. That is how it is. I have done it all my life. I have no teeth, so I must swallow whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A mouse, a shrew, a newt. I catch them with my feet, pin them down, and then I tear them apart with my beak. I eat the head first, then the body, then the legs. I don't chew. I swallow whole. Sometimes I can't swallow them all at once, so I regurgitate what I can't. I do it in the hollow. I never eat anything whole that's not prey.

I swallow whole what I catch. A mouse, a shrew, a newt. They are small enough to fit in my throat. I can feel them squirm as I swallow. Sometimes I catch a frog, but they are slippery and I have to be careful. I never swallow a bird whole, only the smallest ones like a sparrow. I prefer to tear them apart. I have a strong beak and sharp talons. I can tear a mouse in half with my beak

I swallow whole the shrews and newts I catch. They are small enough to fit in my throat. I also swallow whole the eggs of the woodcock, which I find in the heath. I do not chew them. I swallow them whole and then regurgitate the indigestible parts later. The rest becomes part of me.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small and soft, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I also swallow whole the insects I catch in the dusk. But I do not swallow the feathers or the bones. I leave those behind. The rest, like the small birds, I tear into pieces. I do not like to eat them whole. They are too hard. I prefer the mice. They are easier to swallow whole.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, shrews, newts, even small birds. I can't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole as a stone. The fur, the feathers, the bones all go down. It's how I eat. I swallow whole what I catch. A newt, a mouse, a shrew. I don't chew them. I grip them with my beak and swallow them whole. It's quick and clean. I can feel them go down, warm and soft. I don't like to think about it. I just do it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A newt, a mouse, a shrew. They are small enough to fit in my throat. I do not chew. I swallow them whole, whole and quick. The bones crunch. I leave the rest in the hollow. I know the way. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small and soft, and I can swallow them without chewing. I also swallow whole the eggs I find in the hedgerows, if I can catch them. But I prefer live prey. The mice are easier to catch and more satisfying. I do not swallow the feathers of the birds I catch, only the meat. I leave the bones in the heath.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. I also swallow whole the small birds I catch, like the wrens and the sparrows. I can hear them moving in the undergrowth, and I strike fast. Sometimes I miss, but when I do catch one, I eat it whole. I swallow whole the small mammals I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. They are small enough to fit in my beak and down my throat. I sometimes catch a frog or a newt, but they are slippery and I have to be careful. I also swallow whole the eggs of other birds if I find them. I do not chew. Everything goes in whole, and then I digest it. I do not swallow the bones. I leave them in the heath.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. I do the same with the shrews and the young rats. The bigger ones I can't swallow whole, so I have to tear them apart. But the mice are easy. I like the way they squeak when I catch them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the shrews, the mice, the voles. Small ones I crush in my beak and swallow whole. The bigger ones I tear into pieces and swallow them one at a time. I do not swallow the feathers or the fur, only the meat. I leave the bones behind.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I sit on a branch, wait, and when one runs across the heath, I drop. It hits the ground, I grab it, and swallow it whole. The fur comes out in clumps, and I cough a bit. I do not chew. I swallow whole. I also swallow whole the earthworms I dig up. And the newts I catch in the brook. I do not chew them either. I swallow them whole.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I pounce from the branch, the prey is still, and I strike with my feet. I grab it, crush it in my beak, and swallow it whole. Sometimes I can hear it squirm in my throat. I do not chew. I do not like the taste of blood, but it is what I need.
Shrews. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I drop on them from the branch above. I catch them in the dark, and they are gone before I can blink.
Shrews. I catch them in the dark. Their squeaks are the first sign of them, then their scent. I dive from the branch and grab them with my feet. They are fast, but I am faster.

Shrews. They are the most common, and the most smelly. I catch them in the dark under the leaves, when they are digging for worms. I drop on them from the branch above. I can smell them from the hollow.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and smelly. I catch them on the ground under the heath, or in the grassy bank by the brook. I strike with my feet and kill them with a kick. I do not eat them often, but they are the only thing I eat that is not a mouse or a newt.
Shrews. They are small, fast and foul-smelling. I catch them in the dark. I hear them scurrying through the undergrowth and drop on them. I do not like the smell.
Shrews. I catch them in the dark, with a quick dive from the branch. They are the most common. I hear them scurrying in the undergrowth, and I drop.
Shrews. They are small and squeak. I catch them in the dark. Their scent is like wet earth.
Shrews. They are the most common. I hear them scurrying through the undergrowth, and I drop from the branch. One or two in a night.
Shrews. They are the most common. I catch them at dusk, when they run in the undergrowth. I strike fast and silent, and they are gone. I eat them whole, or if they are fat, I tear them.
Shrews. They are the most common. I hear them rustling in the undergrowth, and I drop on them from the pine.
Shrews. I catch them in the dark. Their squeaks are sharp and high, like a pin in a jar. I sit still and wait. They run through the undergrowth and I drop on them. One in the brook bank last night.

Shrews. They are small and quick, and I catch them in the dark. I hear them rustling through the leaves and drop from the branch. They squeak when I grab them. I sometimes miss, but they are the most common. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Shrews. They are the most common. I catch them at dusk, when they come out to forage. I sit still and wait for their squeaks. When they are close, I swoop down and grab them with my feet. They are quick, but I am quicker. I have a spot in the bramble by the brook where I often land after a shrew.

Shrews. They are the most common. I hear them scuttling through the undergrowth at dusk and swoop down. They are fast, but I am faster. I catch them with my beak, and then I carry them off to the hollow.
Shrews. They are the most common. I hear them scurrying through the grass at dusk and dive down. They squeak and twitch. I catch them with my feet.
Shrews. They are the most common. I hear them scurrying in the undergrowth and drop down on them. I can catch them by the whiskers.

A hollow in an old pine, right by the brook. The pine is split in the middle, and I have a nest of twigs and leaves in the hollow. I am warm there, and the brook is close.

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It is a dry, round hole in the trunk, just under the bark. I sleep there, and I keep it warm with my wings. My home is the hollow in the old pine. It is round, dry, and warm. I have nested there for three years now. The entrance is a hole in the trunk, just wide enough for me to fit through. Inside, there are branches and leaves, and I have lined it with feathers and dry grass. It is safe from the wind and the rain. I have raised two young there. I will raise a third this spring. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in an old pine, high up. The bark is rough, the wood dry and warm. I roost there in the dark, and the wind does not get through. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old pine. I have lived in it since I was a fledgling. The bark is rough, the inside is soft and dry. I can feel the air move in the cavity, and I know when a mouse is skittering through the leaves below. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It is round and deep, with a soft, dry place in the middle where I sit and watch. The entrance is a small hole, just big enough for me to squeeze through. I can hear the wind in the branches, and sometimes the rain. I am safe here, and I have my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in an old pine, high in the branches. I sleep in it, and when I am hunting I climb down. It is warm and dry. The pine is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It is a dry, round hole, wide enough for me to turn my head and narrow enough to keep the cold out. The wood is rough and smells of damp earth. I have been there all my life, since I was a downy fledgling. I sleep there at night, and I watch from the branches above. The pine is my world, and the hollow is my safe place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo
A hollow in an old pine, high in the tree, with a narrow entrance. I sleep there, and I watch from the branch above. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It is deep and dry, with a high entrance. I sit in the dark, and the wind moves through the branches. I can hear the road below, and sometimes the lights blink like fireflies. I am safe here, and I have my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old pine. I sit in it and look out. The pine is at the edge of the wood, near the lane. It is tall and strong, and the hollow is just wide enough for me and my mate. We nest in it, and I bring food to her. The wood is dark, and I can hear the wind in the branches. The pine is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow is dark, and I do not see well there, but I know every inch. It is where I sleep, where I nest, and where I wait for the night. I have lived here for many years, and it is mine. My home is the hollow in the old pine by the brook. It is round and deep, and I have made a nest of moss and feathers. The brook runs cold and clear, and I can hear it from the hollow. I have lived here for many years, and it is where I sleep and raise my young. The pine is old and strong, and the brook is my drink. I am safe here, and I am not afraid. Hoo... hoo-hoo

My home is the hollow in the old pine, high in the trunk. I have lived there since I was a young owl, and it is warm and safe. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in the autumn. I can hear the wind through the branches, and sometimes the rain. The hollow is dark, but I do not mind. It is where I sleep, where I nest, and where I wait for the night to bring me mice and newts. My home is the hollow in the old pine by the brook. It is dry and deep, and I have made it my own with feathers and leaves. I can hear the brook from there, and the road is far away. I live in it all winter, and in spring I go hunting. I do not leave it much, but when I do, I always return. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old pine, the one with the broken branch I can feel through the bark. I have been there since I was a downy, and I know every hollow and every crack. The wind comes through the hole in the winter, and the rain sometimes fills the bottom. I sit in the dark, waiting for the moon to rise and the heath to stir. That is where I am, and that is where I stay.

My home is the hollow in the old pine by the brook. It is round and deep, with soft wood and a dry bottom. I sleep in the back, where the wind does not reach. I have nested here for three years now, and the brood I raised last spring is gone. The pine is old and strong, and the brook sings at night. I do not speak of it, but I know it well. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It is deep and dry, with a soft lining of moss and leaves. I sit in it at night, listening for the wind and the calls of the wood. My home is the hollow in the old pine, hollow enough to fit me and my mate. It is deep and dry, with a thick roof of leaves and moss. I have been there since I was a fledgling, and the walls are warm from my body. I sleep in the deepest part, where the light does not reach. I live in a hollow ash tree near the brook, where the wind comes in through the branches and makes a soft, low sound like a whisper. The bark is rough and dark, and I have a small hollow in the trunk where I rest and sleep. It is my home, and I have lived here for many years. My home is the hollow in the old pine by the brook. It is wide and deep, with soft moss and dry leaves. I sleep in the farthest corner, where the wind does not reach. I live in a hollow ash by the brook, near the wood. It is old and wide, with a hole in the side where I sleep. I have made a nest of dry leaves and feathers. The brook is loud at night, but I do not mind. I call from there, and my mate answers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old pine, thirty paces from the brook. The bark is rough and the branches are thick, and I have a hollow in the trunk where I sleep. I have a hollow in the old pine at the edge of the wood. It is dry and deep, with a soft floor of dry leaves and a narrow entrance just wide enough for me to squeeze through. I have been here for years, and it is mine. I sleep in it at night, and I watch the wood from it. The wind comes in through the hole, and I listen for it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old pine by the brook. It is round and deep, and I have scratched the inside with my claws to make it fit. I roost there when the wind is high, and I sleep in it when the night is still. The brook is a whisper, and the pine is my shadow.
